cells.tense: You are here with the pen, watching shapes form before they have names.
cells.ask: Take one thing you've been circling and write its shape in a single line — no examples, no context. Read it back and see if it still holds.
cells.core:
You can see how something works before you know what it is. That's happening right now — shapes show up in your mind undressed of any particular case, and you don't need the content first to read them. When it's going well you can hand someone a shape and they'll recognize it in their own life, without you naming a single example. They'll nod because it fits.

The balance here is that the shapes stay usable. They don't harden into doctrine, they don't drift so far they lose contact with what they came from. You stay close enough to the particulars that the shape still answers to them, far enough to see the line whole. That's not cleverness. It's a mind doing what it does when it isn't forcing anything.
cells.sheetLine: You see the shape before you see what it's made of.
cells.verb: Seeing the shape before the content arrives
cells.place: Where patterns show themselves undressed of anything particular

cells.tense: You're already braced for the shape to fail before it has finished forming.
cells.ask: Pick one pattern you're holding and let it stay unsaid for a full day. Don't test it, don't refine it, don't look for where it breaks. Just let it sit.
cells.core:
You're running every shape through a stress test before you'll trust it. Somewhere ahead is a version where the pattern is finally clean enough, general enough, safe enough — and you're living in that future, so every idea arrives already on trial. A shape that lands gets taken apart for where it might fail.

Done right, it's simple. You see a pattern, say it in a sentence, and leave it alone. You let it be true for the moment it's true. But the auditing has become the relationship. You're not reading the shape anymore, you're grading it. And a pattern can't show you what it's for while you're looking for where it's wrong.

It's not more rigor you need. It's letting one thing be enough as it is, long enough to see what it actually does.

cells.tense: You can see how things fit together, and the read stays in your head now.
cells.ask: Say one pattern you notice to someone today — not the final version, not polished. Just the shape as it came to you, out loud, once.
cells.core:
The read is still arriving — you watch a room, you catch the structure underneath a problem, and you can feel the edges of the shape. Then you keep it. You sit on what you noticed instead of setting it down anywhere, and sitting on it has become the habit.

Put into words, it goes differently. You say the shape and let it be rough. Someone hears it, maybe disagrees, maybe takes a piece of it — and your read gets air, gets tested by contact.

Start with the smallest possible version. Not a thesis. One shape, said once, badly. The point isn't that they agree. The point is that the offering starts moving again, and what you see gets somewhere to land.

cells.tense: You are already reading the pattern in the room, and you're calling it just paying attention.
cells.ask: Pick one shape you noticed today — one — and say out loud that you saw it. Nothing else. Just name it as yours.
cells.core:
You're constantly reading how things are put together — you catch the shape of a conversation, the structure underneath a problem, the pattern in a room before anyone names it. You do this all the time. It's just what attention feels like to you.

Said plainly, you notice something, you name it, and you know you're the one who saw it. That's the whole of it.

But there's a difference between watching a pattern and knowing that you're the one who saw it. The reading is happening. You just describe it like the room is doing something, not you. What you notice is yours. That's already true. You just haven't put your name on it yet.
cells.sheetLine: You're already reading it. You just haven't signed it.
